paragraphs.text:
Of Our Father Among the Saints Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria: To Marcellinus, on the Interpretation of the Psalms.

1. I admire your resolve in Christ, my dear Marcellinus. You are bearing the present trial well, though you have suffered much in it, and you are not neglecting your discipline. When I asked the man who brought your letter how you were getting on after your illness, I learned that you give your leisure to the whole of divine Scripture, but that you read the book of Psalms most often of all, and are eager to grasp the meaning contained in each psalm. I commend you for this, since I too have a great love for this book, as for the whole of Scripture. Indeed, being of that mind, I once met a certain studious old man, and I want to write down for you too what he, who knew the Psalter well, told me about it; for his account has a certain charm and persuasiveness, together with good sense. This is what he said:

2. "All our Scripture, my son, both old and new, is inspired by God and useful for teaching, as it is written. But the book of Psalms offers something especially worth noticing to those who pay attention. Each book serves and proclaims its own particular message: the Pentateuch, for example, tells of the origin of the world and the deeds of the patriarchs, the exodus of Israel from Egypt, and the ordering of the Law; the Triteuch tells of the allotment of the land, the deeds of the judges, and the genealogy of David; the books of Kingdoms and Chronicles tell the deeds of the kings; Ezra tells of the release from captivity and the return of the people, and the rebuilding of the temple and the city; the...

(1) Ed. reads: "Of all."

...Jacob from a barbarous people, Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion. He also sings of these things in the hundred and fourth: He sent Moses his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen. He set among them the words of his signs and of his wonders in the land of Ham. He sent darkness, and it grew dark, and they rebelled against his words. He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish. Their land swarmed with frogs, even in the chambers of their kings. He spoke, and there came dog-flies and gnats throughout all their borders. In short, one can find this whole psalm, and the hundred and fifth as well, written about these same events. The matters of the priesthood and the tabernacle he proclaims in the twenty-eighth psalm, "at the going out of the tabernacle": Bring to the Lord, you sons of God, bring to the Lord young rams, bring to the Lord glory and honor.

4. The events of Joshua son of Nun and of the Judges he points to in a way in the hundred and sixth, where he says: And they founded cities to dwell in, and sowed fields, and planted vineyards. For it was under Joshua that the land of promise was given to them. And when he says repeatedly in the same psalm, And they cried to the Lord in their affliction, and he saved them from their distresses, he is indicating the book of Judges; for at that time, when they cried out, he raised up judges at the proper time and saved the people from those who afflicted them. The events of Kingdoms he sings of in a way in the nineteenth, saying: Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will be made great in the name of the Lord our God. They were hobbled and fell, but we rose and stood upright. Lord, save the king, and hear us on whatever day we call upon you. The events of Ezra he sings in the hundred and twenty-fifth, one of the Songs of Ascents: When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like people comforted; and again in the hundred and twenty-first: I was glad when they said to me, Let us go into the house of the Lord. Our feet were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem. Jerusalem, built as a city whose fellowship is joined together; for there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, as a testimony for Israel.

5. And he points to the matters of the Prophets in almost every psalm. Concerning the coming of the Savior, and that he who comes will be God, he says this in the forty-ninth psalm: The Lord, our God, will come openly, and will not keep silence; and in the hundred and seventeenth: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. We have blessed you from the house of the Lord. The Lord is God, and he has appeared to us. That he is the Word of the Father he sings thus in the hundred and sixth: He sent his Word and healed them, and rescued them from their corruptions. For the God who comes is himself also the Word who is sent. And knowing that this Word is the Son of God, he sings the voice of the Father in the forty-fourth psalm: My heart has poured forth a good Word; and again in the hundred and

ninth: From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you. For what else could one call the offspring of the Father but his Word and Wisdom? And knowing that it was he to whom the Father said, Let there be light, and Let there be a firmament, and all the rest, this book also contains the words: By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their host by the breath of his mouth.

6. Nor was he unaware that the Christ himself would come; indeed he speaks of this above all in the forty-fourth psalm: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. And so that no one might think he came only in appearance, he indicates that he would become man, and that he is the one through whom all things came to be, saying in the eighty-sixth: Mother Zion will say, A man, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her. This is the same as saying: And the Word was God; all things came into being through him; and the Word became flesh. For this reason, knowing also of the birth from a Virgin, he did not keep silent about it, but at once gives a hint of it in the forty-fourth psalm, saying: Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house, for the king has desired your beauty. This again is like what Gabriel said: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you. For having called him Christ, he at once also made known his human birth from the Virgin, saying, Hear, O daughter. Notice that Gabriel calls Mary by name, since he is a stranger to her by birth, whereas David fittingly addresses her as daughter, since she comes from his own seed.

(2) Ed.: "In the thirty-second."

...which he bore, he who says through Isaiah, He himself took our infirmities; and while we say in the hundred and thirty-seventh psalm, The Lord will repay on my behalf, the Spirit also says in the seventy-first: And he will save the children of the poor and humble the slanderer, for he has rescued the poor man from the hand of the powerful, and the needy man who had no helper.

8. For this reason he also foretells his bodily ascent into heaven, and says in the twenty-third: Lift up your gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall come in; and in the forty-[?]: God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet. He also announces his session, saying in the hundred and ninth: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet; and in the ninth he proclaims the destruction of the devil as well: You sat on a throne, you who judge righteously; you rebuked the nations, and the ungodly man perished. Nor did he hide the fact that he received all judgment from the Father; rather, he foretells that he will come as judge of all, in the seventy-first: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son, to judge your people in righteousness and your poor with justice; and in the forty-ninth he says: He will summon the heaven above, and the earth, to judge his people. And the heavens will declare his righteousness, for God is judge; and in the eighty-first: God has taken his stand in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges gods. And indeed the calling of the Gentiles can be learned from this book in many places, but above all from the forty-sixth: Clap your hands, all you nations, shout to God with a voice of rejoicing; and in the seventy-first: The Ethiopians will fall down before him, and his enemies will lick the dust; the kings of Tarshish and the islands will bring gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Saba will offer gifts; and all the kings of the earth will worship him, all the nations will serve him. These things are sung in the Psalms, and they are also foretold in each of the other books.

9. Again, he said, he was well aware that the same things concerning the Savior are especially signified in every book of Scripture; this is the message of them all, and the one harmony of the Spirit. For just as the contents of the other books can be found in this one, so the contents of this one are often found in the others. Moses writes a song, Isaiah sings, and Habakkuk prays with a song. And again, in every book one can see prophecy and legislation and history. For the same Spirit is upon all; and according to the distribution he makes to each, each one ministers the grace given to him

(5) Ed.: "common."

and fulfills it, whether it is prophecy, or legislation, or the record of history, or the grace of the psalms. But since it is one and the same Spirit to whom all the distributions belong, while he himself is by nature undivided, the whole is present in each, while the manifestations and distributions of the Spirit come to each according to their ministry. So, as the need at hand requires, each often ministers the word as the Spirit supplies it. Thus, as I said before, Moses the lawgiver sometimes prophesies and sings; the prophets, while prophesying, sometimes give commands: Wash yourselves, become clean, and, Wash your heart from wickedness, O Jerusalem; and sometimes they narrate history, Daniel the story of Susanna, and Isaiah that of the Rabshakeh and Sennacherib. So too the [book] of the Psalms [?] ... of the Savior, as was said before.

10. Such a grace of the Spirit, then, will be common to all, and it is to be found at work in each, and the same in all, as need demands and the Spirit wills. In this kind of need, more or less makes no difference, so long as each one tirelessly fulfills and completes his own ministry. Even so, the book of Psalms has in turn a certain grace of its own and a distinction all its own. Besides the other things in which it is related to the other books and shares with them, it has this marvel peculiar to itself: it contains, described and portrayed within itself, the movements of every soul, with their changes and corrections. So whoever wishes may draw from it as from a boundless store, and come to understand, and so shape himself, for it is written there. In the other books one only hears the Law commanding what one must do and what one must not do; one listens to prophecies only so as to know about the coming Savior; and one pays attention to histories, from which one can learn the deeds of the kings and of the saints. But in the book of Psalms, besides learning these things, the hearer also perceives and is taught the movements of his own soul. And further, whatever he is suffering and whatever grips him, he can again find in this book the pattern of words for it, so that he does not merely hear and pass on, but is taught how to heal his affliction by what he says and does. In the other books too there are prohibitions forbidding what is evil, but in this one it is also portrayed how one must abstain from it. For example...

(8) Ed.: "In himself."

...the command is to repent, and to repent is to cease from sin; but here it is also portrayed how to repent and what one should say in repentance. Again, Paul has said: Affliction produces endurance in the soul, and endurance produces tested character, and tested character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame. But in the Psalms it is written and engraved how one must bear afflictions, what one should say while afflicted and what after the afflictions, how each person is tested, and what the words of those who hope in the Lord are. Again, there is a commandment to give thanks in everything; but the Psalms teach what one should say when giving thanks. Then, when we hear from others, All who want to live godly lives will be persecuted, from the Psalms we are taught how we should cry out when we flee, and what words we should offer to God when we are persecuted and when we have been rescued after the persecution. We are commanded to bless the Lord and to give him thanks; but in the Psalms we are shown how we should praise the Lord, and with what words we may fittingly give thanks. And so in every case one would find the divine songs suited to us and to our movements and conditions.

11. And there is something else remarkable about the Psalms. In the other books, those who read aloud what the saints say, and the things they speak about, are reciting matters concerning those about whom they were written; and those who listen consider themselves different from the people the word is about, and the deeds recounted move them only so far as to admire them and wish to imitate them. But whoever takes up this book, while he goes through the prophecies about the Savior with admiration and reverence, as he usually does in the other Scriptures, reads the other psalms as his own words; and the one who listens is pierced to the heart as though he himself were speaking, and is moved by the words of the songs as though they were his own (9). For clarity's sake one should not hesitate, as the blessed Apostle says, to go back and say the same thing again. There are a great many words of the patriarchs, spoken by them as their own; Moses spoke, and God answered; Elijah and Elisha, sitting on Mount Carmel, called upon the Lord and constantly said, As the Lord lives, before whom I stand today. And the words of the other holy prophets are first and foremost about the Savior, and then a great many were addressed to the nations and to Israel. And yet no one would ever speak the words of the patriarchs as his own, nor would anyone dare to imitate and speak Moses' own words, or Abraham's words about his home-born servant and about Ishmael and the great Isaac. Even if the same need and necessity overtook someone, who would dare to speak them as his own? And even if one feels for those who suffer, and is at times seized by a longing for better things, he would never say, as

(9) Ed.: "since they are his own."

Moses did, Show yourself to me; or again, If you will forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of your book which you have written. Nor would anyone, taking the words of the prophets as his own, blame or praise those who do things like the deeds those prophets blamed and praised; nor would anyone imitate the saying, As the Lord lives, before whom I stand today, and speak it as his own. For whoever reads those books is plainly speaking the words not as his own, but as the words of the saints and of those they describe. But the Psalms, remarkably, are different: apart from the prophecies about the Savior and the nations, the one who recites them speaks the rest as his own words, and each person sings them as though written about himself. He does not take them and go through them as though someone else were speaking or as though they referred to someone else; rather, he feels as if he were speaking about himself, and whatever is said, he offers to God as though he himself had done it and were speaking from his own heart. He will not hold back from these with reverent caution, as he would from the words of the patriarchs, of Moses, and of the other prophets; on the contrary, the one who sings them boldly speaks them as his own and as written about himself. For the Psalms include both the one who has kept the commandment and the one who has broken it, and the conduct of each. And every person must be included among these, and speak the words written about one or the other, either as one who has kept the commandment or as one who has broken it.

12. It seems to me that for the one who sings them the Psalms become like a mirror, so that he perceives himself and the movements of his own soul in them, and recites them with that understanding. For the one who hears the reader takes in the song as spoken about himself: either, convicted by his conscience, he will be pierced to the heart and repent, or, hearing of hope in God and of the help given to believers, he rejoices as though such grace had come to him, and begins to give thanks to God. So when someone sings the third psalm with his own afflictions in view, he considers the words of the psalm to be his own; and then he recites the eleventh and the sixteenth as expressing his own confidence and prayer, and the fiftieth as though he himself were speaking the words of his own repentance. And when someone sings the fifty-third, the fifty-fifth, the fifty-sixth and the hundred and forty-first, he does not feel as though someone else were being persecuted, but as one who is himself suffering, and he sings these words to the Lord as his own. In short, each psalm has been spoken and composed by the Spirit in such a way that, as was said before, the movements of our soul can be perceived in them, and all of them are spoken as if about us, and are our own words, to remind us of the movements within us and to correct our way of life. For what the psalmists said can also serve as patterns and models for us.

13. This too is the grace of the Savior. Having become man for our sake, he offered his own body to death on our behalf, to free all from death; and his heavenly and

well-pleasing way of life, wishing to show it to us, he modeled in himself, so that no one might any longer be easily deceived by the enemy, since we have as a pledge of security the victory he won over the devil on our behalf. That is why he not only taught but also did what he taught, so that each person might hear him speaking and also, seeing as in an image, take from him the example of how to act, as he hears: Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart. One could find no more perfect teaching of virtue than the one the Lord modeled in himself. Whether it is forbearance, or love for humanity, or goodness, or courage, or mercy, or righteousness, one will find it all realized in him, so that nothing in the way of virtue is lacking to anyone who contemplates this human life of his. Knowing this, Paul said: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. The lawgivers among the Greeks have a gift that goes no further than words; but the Lord, being truly Lord of all and caring for what he made, not only gives laws but has given himself as a pattern, so that those who wish may know how to put them into practice. That is why, even before his coming among us, he made this sound forth in those who sang the psalms: so that, just as he showed in himself the pattern of the earthly and the heavenly man, so too anyone who wishes may learn from the Psalms the movements and dispositions of souls, finding in them both the healing and

14. To put it more persuasively still: the whole of divine Scripture is a teacher of virtue and of true faith, but the book of Psalms also offers, in a way, a picture of how souls should conduct themselves. Just as someone going in to see a king is schooled in both his bearing and his words, so that he is not thrown out as ill-mannered for speaking otherwise, so the divine book first reminds, through reading, the one who runs after virtue and wishes to understand the Savior's way of life in the body of the movements of the soul, and only then shapes and teaches those who read such words. Now, to note this first about the book, some psalms are spoken as narrative, some as exhortation, some as prophecy, some as prayer, and some as thanksgiving. Those in narrative form are 18, 43, 48, 49, 72, 76, 77, 88, 106, 113, 126, 136. Those in the form of prayer are 16, 67, 89, 101, 131, 141. Those in the form of petition, prayer and supplication are 5, 6, [?], 12, 15, 24, 27, 30, 34, 37, 42, 53, 54, [?], 82, 85, 87, 137, 139,
The one in the form of petition and thanksgiving is 138. Those in the form of petition alone are 3, 25, 68, 69, 70, 73, 78 [?], 79, 108, 122, 129 [?], 130.

[?] Those with [?] words are 22 and 26, 38, 39, 41, 61, [?], 83, [?], [?], 151 [?]. The reproving ones are 57 and 81. Some speak words of a hymn: 45 and 64. One speaks words of shouting and about the resurrection: 65. And another speaks only words of shouting: 99 [?]. Since the Psalms are arranged in this way, readers can find in each of them, as I said before, the movements and the state of their own soul, and likewise the pattern and the teaching for each situation. They can learn what to say in order to please the Lord, and with what words they can correct themselves and give thanks to the Lord, so that whoever says such things does not fall into impiety. For we shall have to give an account to the Judge not only for our deeds but also for every idle word. So if you wish to call someone blessed, you have the way to do it, the reason, and the words to use: Psalms 1, 31, 40, 111, 118 and 127. If you wish to condemn the plot of the Jews against the Saviour, you have the second psalm. If you are persecuted by your own people and many have risen up against you, say Psalm 3. If, afflicted in this way, you have called on the Lord and been heard, and you wish to give thanks, sing Psalm 4, and 74, and 114. And if you still see the wicked wanting to lie in wait for you, and you want your prayer to be heard, rise early

and sing Psalm 5 in the morning. If you sense the Lord's threat and see that you are troubled by it, you can say Psalms 6 and 37. If people plot against you, as Ahithophel did against David, and someone reports it to you, sing Psalm 7 and put your trust in God who rescues you. 16. If you see the Saviour's grace spread out everywhere and the human race saved, and you wish to address the Lord, sing Psalm 8. Or again, if you wish to sing a song for the winepresses in thanksgiving to the Lord, you have Psalm 8 again, and 83 [?]. For the overthrow of the enemy and the salvation of creation, do not boast in yourself; knowing that the Son of God has accomplished this, say Psalm 9, which was spoken about him. If someone is set on troubling you greatly, keep your confidence in the Lord and sing Psalm 10. When you see the arrogance of the many and wickedness growing, so that nothing holy is left among people, take refuge in the Lord and say Psalm 11. When the enemies' plotting drags on, do not lose heart as though God had forgotten you, but call on the Lord by singing Psalm 12. When you hear people blaspheming against Providence, do not share in their impiety, but intercede with God and say Psalms 13 and 52. And if you wish to learn what kind of person the citizen of the kingdom of heaven is, sing Psalm 14. 17. Do you need to pray because of those who oppose you and surround your soul? Sing Psalm 16, and 85, and 87, and 140. Do you wish to learn how Moses prayed? You have Psalm 89. Have you been saved from your enemies and rescued from your persecutors? Then you too sing Psalm 17. Do you marvel at the order of creation, the grace of Providence within it, and the holy commandments of the law? Sing Psalms 18 and 23. When you see people in affliction, comfort them, praying for them and saying to them the words of Psalm 19. Do you see that the Lord is shepherding you and leading you on a good path? Rejoice at this and sing Psalm 22. Are enemies surrounding you? Lift up your soul to God and say Psalm 24, and you will see them sinning to no purpose. Do the enemies persist, their hands full of nothing but blood, seeking to drag you off and destroy you? Do not leave the judgment to a human being, for everything human is open to suspicion. Instead ask God to be the judge, for he alone is just, and say the words of Psalm 25, and 34, and 42. If they attack more fiercely and the enemies become a multitude like armies, despising you as not yet anointed and so wanting to make war on you, do not cower, but sing Psalm 26. Since human nature is weak, if the plotters grow shameless again, cry out to God with the words of Psalm 27, so that you need not spend your time on them. If you wish to learn how to make an offering of thanksgiving to the Lord, understand it spiritually and sing Psalm 28. And when you dedicate your house, both the soul that receives the Lord and the bodily house in which you live in the body, give thanks and say Psalm 29 and the one among the Songs of Ascents

18. When you see yourself hated and persecuted for the sake of the truth by all your friends and relatives, do not lose heart, whether over them or over yourself. If you see your acquaintances turning away from you, do not cower, but withdraw from them, keep your eyes on what is to come, and sing Psalm 30. When you see people being baptized and redeemed from corruptible birth, and you marvel at God's love for humanity, sing Psalm 31 over them. When you want to sing psalms with many others, gather together righteous men of upright life and say Psalm 32. If you have fallen among enemies, escaped them wisely and slipped out of their plot, and you wish to give thanks, call the gentle together and sing Psalm 33 in their presence. If you see how eagerly the lawless contend for evil, do not think that wickedness is in them by nature, as the heretics say. Say Psalm 35 instead, and you will see that they themselves are responsible for their sin. If you see the wicked doing many lawless things and exalting themselves over the lowly, and you wish to warn others not to pay attention to them or envy them, since they are quickly snuffed out, say Psalm 36 both to yourself and to others. 19. And if you yourself have resolved to watch over yourself, and you see the enemy attacking (for that is when he rises up most against such people), and you wish to anoint yourself against him, sing Psalm 38. If you endure afflictions while enemies attack, and you wish to learn the benefit of endurance, sing Psalm 39. When you see many poor and needy people and wish them to receive mercy, you can commend those who have already shown mercy and urge the others to do the same by saying Psalm 40. Then, if you have a great longing for God and hear your enemies taunting you, do not be troubled. Understand the immortal fruit of such longing, comfort your soul with hope in God, lightening and soothing by that hope the griefs it bears in this life, and say Psalm 41. If you wish to keep recalling God's benefits to our fathers, the exodus from Egypt and the time in the wilderness, how God is good and human beings ungrateful, you have Psalm 43,

and 77, and 88, and 104, and 105, and 106, and 113. If you have taken refuge in God and been saved from the afflictions that came upon you, and you wish to give thanks to God and tell of the love he has shown you, you have Psalm 45. 20. Have you sinned, and in your shame do you repent and ask for mercy? You have the words of confession and repentance in Psalm 50. If you have been slandered to a wicked king and see the devil boasting over you, withdraw and say the words of Psalm 51. When you are persecuted, and some slander you and want to hand you over, as the Ziphites and the foreigners did to David, do not despair. Trust in the Lord, praise him, and say the words of Psalms 53 and 55. And if the persecutor

comes rushing in and unknowingly enters the cave where you are hiding, do not cower even then. For you have oracles for comfort in such straits, and words of inscription, in Psalm 56 and in Psalm 141. If the plotter orders your house to be watched and you escape, offer your thanks to the Lord, writing it on your soul as on pillars, a memorial that you were not destroyed, and say the words of Psalm 58. If your enemies taunt and oppress you, and those who seem to be your friends slander you with idle chatter, and you are grieved for a little while in your meditation, you can still be comforted by praising God yourself and saying the words of Psalm 54. Against hypocrites and those who boast to your face, say Psalm 57 [?] to shame them. Against those who rush savagely at you and want to take your life, set your submission to your God and take courage. For the more they rage, the more you must submit to the Lord, and say the words of Psalm 61. If you are persecuted and go off into the wilderness, do not be afraid as though you were alone there. You have God there, so rise early to seek him and sing Psalm 62. If the enemies terrify you and do not stop lying in wait, but search out every means against you, even if they are many, do not give way, for their blows will be like children's arrows. Sing for yourself Psalm 63, and 64, and 69, and 70. 21. When you want to praise the Lord, sing the words of Psalm 64. If you wish to teach some people about the resurrection, sing the words of Psalm 65. When you ask God for mercy, praise him by singing Psalm 66. When you see the wicked thriving in peace and living as they please, while the righteous are afflicted, say the words of Psalm 72, so that you do not stumble or waver. When God is angry with his people, you have wise words of comfort for this in Psalm 73. When you need to give thanks, sing Psalm 9, 74, 91 [?], 104, 105, 106, 107 [?], 110, 117, 135 and 137. If you wish to put the Greeks and the heretics to shame, because the knowledge of God is not found among them but only in the Catholic Church, you can, with understanding, sing and say the words of Psalm 75 [?]. If your enemies have seized the ways of escape beforehand and you are sorely afflicted, do not despair even if you are troubled, but pray. And if you cry out and are heard, give thanks to God with the words of Psalm 76. If the enemies persist and break in, defile the house of God, kill the saints and throw their bodies to the birds of the sky, do not be dragged along and cower before their cruelty. Suffer with those who suffer, and intercede with God, saying Psalm 78.

22. If you wish to sing to the Lord at a feast, call together the servants of God and sing the words of Psalms 80 and 94. When the enemies have once more gathered from every side, threatening the house of God and making pacts against true religion,

you have the words of Psalm 82 as an anchor of hope, so that you do not lose heart because of their numbers and power. If you see the house of God and his eternal dwellings and long for them, as the Apostle did, then you too say Psalm 83. When at last the wrath has ceased and the captivity has ended, if you wish to give thanks, you have the words of Psalms 84 and 125 to say. If you wish to know how the Catholic Church differs from the schisms, and to put the schismatics to shame, you can say what is written in Psalm 86. If you wish to encourage yourself and others in the fear of God, and to show that hope in God does not put us to shame but makes the soul fearless, praise God with the words of Psalm 90. Do you wish to sing on the Sabbath? You have Psalm 91. 23. Do you wish to give thanks on the Lord's Day? You have Psalm 23. Do you wish to sing on Monday? Say the words of Psalm 47. Do you wish to praise God on Friday? You have the praise in Psalm 92. For it was then, when the cross took place, that the house of God was built, though the enemies tried to prevent it. That is why it is fitting then to sing to God a victory song in the words of Psalm 92. If captivity comes and the house is torn down and then built again, sing the words of Psalm 95. When the land has been made secure from those who wage war on it and is at last at rest, and the Lord reigns, if you wish to sing about this, you have Psalm 96. Do you wish to sing on Wednesday? You have Psalm 93. For it was then that the Lord, having been betrayed, began to execute judgment on death and to triumph over it openly. So when you read in the Gospel that on Wednesday the Jews took counsel against the Lord, and you see him then speaking boldly as he takes vengeance on the devil on our behalf, sing the words of that same psalm [?]. Again, if you see the Lord's providence over all things and his lordship, and you wish to instruct some people in faith in him and obedience to him, persuading them first to give thanks, sing Psalm 99. And if you have learned of his power to judge, and that the Lord judges by tempering judgment with mercy, and you wish to draw near to him, you have the words of Psalm 100 for this. 24. Since our nature is weak, if the pressures of life ever make you feel poor and despondent, and you wish to be comforted, you have Psalm 101. And since we ought to give thanks to God through all things and in all things, when you wish to bless him you have Psalms 102 and 103, with which to stir up your soul. Do you wish to praise God and to know how and for what he should be praised, and who ought to offer the praise? You have Psalm 104, and 106, and 134 [?], 145, and 146, and 147 [?], and 148, and 150. Do you have faith, as the Lord said, and do you believe what you speak in prayer? Say Psalm 115. Do you perceive yourself ascending in your conduct, so that you can say, "Forgetting what lies behind, I strain forward to what lies ahead"? For each step forward you have the fifteen Songs of Ascents to say.

25. Have you been taken captive by alien thoughts, felt yourself being carried off, and repented? Stop from now on. Stay where you caught yourself sinning, sit down and weep, as the people did then, saying the words of Psalm 136. If you regard temptations as your testing, and after the temptations you wish to give thanks, you have Psalm 138. Are you hemmed in by enemies again and want to be rescued? Say the words of Psalm 139 [?]. Do you wish to make petition and pray? Sing Psalms 5 and 142. Has an enemy, a tyrant, risen up against the people and against you, as Goliath did against David? Do not cower, but believe as David did, and say the words of Psalm 143. Then, if you marvel at God's benefits to all, and remember the goodness he has shown to you and to everyone, and you wish to bless God for these things, say the words of David, which he himself spoke in Psalm 144. Do you wish to sing to the Lord? You have Psalms 92 and 97 to say. If, though you are young, you are chosen ahead of your brothers for some office, do not exalt yourself over them, but give glory to the Lord who chose you and sing Psalm 151, which is David's own. Do you wish to sing psalms that have the response "Alleluia"? You have Psalms 104, 105, 106, 111, 112, 113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 134, 135, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149, 150, and [?]. When you wish to sing on your own about the Saviour, you will find such things in almost every psalm. But above all you have Psalms 44 and 109, which declare his true begetting from the Father and his coming in the flesh; Psalms 21 and 68, which foretell the divine cross, how great a plot he endured for our sake and how much he suffered; Psalms 2 and 108, which signify the plotting and wickedness of the Jews and the betrayal by Judas Iscariot; and Psalms 20, 49 and 71, which declare his kingdom and his power to judge, his second coming to us in the flesh, and the calling of the nations. Psalm 15 shows his resurrection from the dead, and Psalms 23 and 46 proclaim his ascension into heaven. And by reading Psalms 92, 95 [?], 97 and 98 you will be able to contemplate the benefits the Saviour has won for us through his sufferings. 27. Such, then, is the character of the Book of Psalms and the benefit it offers to people. It has psalms of its own kinds, and, as I said before, in the rest it also contains frequent prophecies about the coming of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ in the body. Nor must we pass over the question of why such words are sung with melody and song. For some of the simple among us, though they believe the words are divinely inspired, still think that the psalms are chanted for the sake of a pleasing sound and to delight the ear. That is not so. Scripture did not seek what is sweet and persuasive. This too was ordained for the benefit of the soul, for every reason but above all for these two. First, it was fitting for divine Scripture to praise God not only in continuous speech but also with a voice drawn out at length.

The writings of the law and the prophets, all the historical books, and the New Testament are spoken as continuous speech; the words of the psalms, odes and songs are uttered at length. In this way it is ensured that people love God with all their strength and power. Second, just as harmony joins the pipes together and produces a single concord, so it is with the soul. Different movements appear in it: there is reasoning in it, and desire, and the spirited part, and from the motion of these comes the activity of the body's members. The Word wishes a person not to be out of tune with himself or at odds with himself. Otherwise he might reason what is best but act basely out of passion, like Pilate, who said, "I find no fault in him," yet went along with the will of the Jews. Or he might desire base things but be unable to do them, like the elders who plotted against Susanna. Or again, he might not commit adultery, yet steal; or not steal, yet murder; or not murder, yet blaspheme. 28. So that no such disorder arises in us, the Word wishes the soul, which has the mind of Christ, as the Apostle said, to take that mind as its guide, and by it to master the passions within it and to govern the members of the body so that they obey reason. Then, as the plectrum is to the harmony, so the person himself becomes a psaltery: he gives his whole attention to the Spirit, obeys in all his members and movements, and serves the will of God. The melodious reading of the Psalms is an image and type of this untroubled, calm state of the thoughts. For just as we make known and express the thoughts of the soul by the words we utter, so the Lord, wishing the melody of the words to be a symbol of the spiritual harmony in the soul, ordained that the odes be sung melodiously and the psalms be read with song. And this is the soul's desire: to be in a good state, as it is written, "Is anyone among you cheerful? Let him sing psalms." In this way whatever is turbulent, rough and disorderly in the soul is smoothed out, and whatever grieves it is healed, as we sing, "Why are you so sorrowful, my soul, and why do you disquiet me?" It will recognize where it has stumbled, saying, "But my feet were almost shaken"; and what is afraid it will strengthen with hope, saying, "The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man can do to me." 29. So those who do not read the divine songs in this way do not sing with understanding. They please themselves, but they incur blame, for "Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner." But those who sing in the way described, so that the melody of the words comes from the rhythm of the soul and its concord with the Spirit, such people

they sing with the tongue, and since they sing with the mind as well, they bring great benefit not only to themselves but also to those who wish to hear them. So the blessed David, singing in this way to Saul, was himself pleasing to God. He drove away Saul's turmoil and frenzied passion and brought calm to his soul. In the same way the priests, by their singing, called the souls of the people to tranquillity and to harmony with those who dance in the heavens. So the reciting of the psalms with melody is not an effort after fine sound. It is a sign of the harmony of the thoughts in the soul, and melodious reading is a symbol of the well-ordered and unstormy state of the mind. Praising God on well-sounding cymbals, the harp and the ten-stringed psaltery was likewise a symbol and a sign: the members of the body are to be duly ordered like strings, the thoughts of the soul are to become like cymbals, and then all of these are to be moved and to live by the sound and the prompting of the Spirit. Then, as it is written, a person lives by the Spirit and puts to death the deeds of the body. For whoever sings well brings his soul into rhythm and leads it, as it were, from inequality to equality. Standing in its natural state, it is not frightened by anything; instead it is filled with good images and gains a greater longing for the good things to come. 30. So then, my child, everyone who reads this book must read all that is in it sincerely, since it is divinely inspired. Then, as if from the fruits of paradise, he must take from it the benefit he sees he needs. For I think that in the words of this book the whole life of human beings, the dispositions of the soul and the movements of the thoughts are measured out and contained, and that nothing beyond these is found among human beings. Perhaps someone needs repentance or confession. Perhaps affliction and temptation have overtaken him, or he has been persecuted, or he has been plotted against and rescued. Perhaps he has become deeply grieved and troubled, or is suffering something like what was described above. Perhaps he sees himself making progress while the enemy is brought to nothing, or he wants to praise, give thanks to and bless the Lord. In every case he has the teaching for it in the divine psalms. Let him choose what is said in them about each of these things. Let him say it as though it had been written about himself, enter into the feeling of what is written, and so offer it up to the Lord. 31. But let no one clothe the psalms in the persuasive words of outsiders, or try to alter or change their wording in any way. Let him simply say and sing what is written, just as it was spoken, so that the holy men who ministered them

Israel, simply by reading the Scriptures, drove out demons and exposed the plots they make against human beings. He therefore said that those who abandon these words deserve every condemnation, as do those who put together persuasive words from outside and then call themselves exorcists by means of them. Such people are really playing games, and they offer themselves to the demons to be mocked, as happened to the Jews, the sons of Sceva, when they too tried to exorcise in this way. When the demons hear such words from people like that, they mock them; but they fear the words of the saints and cannot bear them. For the Lord is in the words of the Scriptures, and because they could not bear him they cried out, “I beg you, do not torment me before the time!” They were burned simply by seeing the Lord present. It was in this way that Paul commanded the unclean spirits, and in this way that the demons were made subject to the disciples. And the hand of the Lord came upon the prophet Elisha, and he prophesied to the three kings about the waters, while the minstrel played at his command. So now too, if anyone cares for those who suffer, let him say these words. He will benefit the sufferer more, and he will show his own faith to be true and firm, so that God, seeing it, will grant complete healing to those in need. The saint knew this when he said in Psalm 118: “I will meditate on your statutes; I will not forget your words”; and again: “Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my sojourning.” For through these they gained salvation, saying: “If your law had not been my meditation, I would have perished in my humiliation.” That is also why Paul made his disciple secure in these things, saying: “Meditate on these things; give yourself to them, so that your progress may be evident.” If you meditate on these things too, and read the psalms in this thoughtful way, then, guided by the Spirit, you will be able to grasp the sense of each one. And you will strive for the kind of life that was lived by the holy, God-inspired men who spoke these words. (9) The edition reads: “will benefit.”

In the Hebrew book of the Psalms, all of them were written down without any numbers added, and in different arrangements: some are joined together and others are divided. For example, the first and second are joined in the Hebrew. And again the ninth, which is a single psalm in our text, is divided into two in the Hebrew. The whole book of Psalms is also divided into five parts. It should be noted that the Psalms are not arranged in the order of historical events. Their order was disturbed over many periods of time, as the book of Kingdoms shows. Idolatry had gained a strong hold over the Jewish nation, and so, it is said, they forgot their ancestral Scriptures. The book of the law of Moses could no longer even be found, and nothing at all of their fathers' piety was preserved among them. They went so far as to kill the prophets who rebuked their impieties, and for this they were first handed over to captivity by the Assyrians. After that, it is said, one of the prophets set himself to collect the Scriptures, and along with the others he gathered the book of Psalms. He did not find them all at once, but at different times, and he placed first those that were found first. That is why David's psalms are not all found in sequence. In between them are psalms of the sons of Korah, of Asaph, of Solomon, of Moses, of Ethan the Israelite and of Heman, and then David's again, all found mixed together and arranged in

the book. They are ordered not by the times when they were spoken, but by the times when they were found. You would find that the same thing has happened in the sections of the prophets as well. The children of the Hebrews say that the untitled psalms after the first and twelfth [?], and also those with a title that does not show whose they are, belong to the author whose name appears in the psalm placed before them. I think the first and second psalms, which are really one, are David's, because all the psalms after them in the first part of the Psalms are his. From the third to the fortieth, all are titled “of David,” and so it seems to me that the first and second are by him as well. The book of the Acts of the Apostles confirms this argument, where it says: “Master, you made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them. By the Holy Spirit, through the mouth of our father David your servant, you said: ‘Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot vain things?’” By these words it clearly states that the second psalm is David's. David's name was probably left off the title because the psalm contains an open prophecy about the Lord, in which it is said: “Against the Lord and against his Christ.” After this, speaking in the person of Christ himself, it adds: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son.’” There are, then, 150 psalms in all. Some think that all of them are by the blessed David, but this is not what the text indicates. All of them are attributed to David, but the titles show whose each psalm is. Four leaders of the singers were chosen, with 288 followers, and psalms are assigned to these four leaders, as the titles also teach. Whenever it says “A psalm for the sons of Korah, Ethan, Asaph and Heman,” it is the sons of Korah, Ethan, Asaph and Heman who sing it. When it says “A psalm of Asaph,” Asaph himself spoke it. When it says “A psalm of Jeduthun,” Jeduthun himself sings it. Whenever it says “of David,” David himself was the speaker. But when it says “to David,” it is spoken by others with reference to David. There are 150 in all: 72 are of David, 9 to David, 12 of Asaph, 12 to the sons of Korah, one of Jeduthun, one of Ethan, one of Heman, one of Solomon, two of Haggai and Zechariah, 39 untitled, and one of Moses, making 150 in all. So we must consider the mystery: why, though there are different singers and not all the psalms are David's, they are all attributed to David. We will not pass over this. They were given his name because he himself was the cause of their existence, for he chose the singers. Since he was their cause, he was judged worthy of this honour, so that everything the singers said should be credited to David.

David was a prophet, and the eyes within him had been opened. He knew that the evil spirits rejoice at the fall of human beings, and that they in turn are grieved and defeated when human beings are set right. So he certainly made his prayers against these spirits in a spiritual sense, turning from the visible enemies to them. If we do not understand the aim of the prophets in this way, we will gain no edification toward gentleness from what they said. Worse, we will take on a harsh disposition, contrary to the teaching of the Gospel, by constantly cursing our enemies instead of loving them, since David says countless times: “Let all my enemies be put to shame and confounded, and let me not be put to shame.” We could not be persuaded that men who were prophets and friends of God said such things, except in the way described above. So wherever the diligent reader finds a prophet uttering curses, he should understand him as turning from the visible enemies to the spiritual ones. For the rest, the ascetic should devote himself to understanding every word.
